opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot, because a big part of my work has been on writing fast kernels, and that's traditionally been a pretty painful process. You're writing CUDA, you're thinking about memory hierarchies, shared memory, registers, tensor cores, all these low-level details. And the reason we've built DSLs like Triton, or more recently things like ThunderKittens and CuTe DSL, is to raise the level of abstraction so that a human expert can be productive without having to manage every single detail by hand.

Now, as language models get better at writing code, the question becomes: who is the DSL for? I think the answer is increasingly going to be both humans and models. And interestingly, a lot of the principles that make a DSL good for humans also make it good for models. You want the right abstractions, you want the primitives to map cleanly onto what the hardware actually does, and you want it to be hard to write something that's subtly wrong. If you have a small set of well-designed building blocks, like tile-level operations, a model can compose those much more reliably than it can write raw CUDA with thousands of ways to shoot yourself in the foot.

The other thing is feedback. Models do really well when there's a tight loop: generate something, compile it, check correctness, measure performance, and iterate. So I think DSLs designed with that in mind, with fast compilation, good error messages, and easy ways to verify correctness against a reference, are going to be really valuable. That's sort of the environment where you can let a model search over a lot of possible implementations.

And longer term, I think there's an interesting question of whether models will push us toward lower-level control again. If the model is good enough, maybe you don't need as much abstraction, and you want to expose more of the hardware so it can find optimizations a human wouldn't bother with. So it's a bit of a moving target. Right now I'd say the sweet spot is abstractions that are high-level enough to be productive but still give you an escape hatch to the hardware when you need it. That's been true for humans, and I suspect it'll be true for models for a while too.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts human expert productivity with models’ strengths: composing well-designed primitives and iterating through a generate, compile, check, and measure loop. It uses those model-specific behaviors to motivate DSL design.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, because the question has kind of flipped on us. For a long time the goal of a DSL was to make it easier for humans to write fast kernels. Triton is the obvious example: you give up some control over the hardware, but you get something a grad student can actually use instead of writing CUDA or PTX by hand. The abstraction was a trade-off made for people.

Now the main author of a lot of this code is increasingly going to be a model, and models have very different strengths and weaknesses than people. A model doesn't get tired writing boilerplate. It doesn't mind if the language is verbose. What it really struggles with is the stuff that's implicit: the hidden performance model, the weird hardware quirks, the "oh, on Hopper you want the TMA and warp specialization, on Blackwell the tensor memory changes the whole picture" kind of knowledge that lives in people's heads and in scattered forum posts.

So my current thinking is that you want the DSL to be as explicit as possible about the things that matter for performance. Make the memory hierarchy visible. Make the asynchrony visible. Make it clear what's running on which part of the chip. That sounds like it's going in the opposite direction of abstraction, but I think it's the right direction for a model, because the model can handle the verbosity and what it needs is a clear, inspectable contract with the hardware. That's a lot of why we've been pushing on things like the CuTe DSL in Python for FlashAttention 4, where you keep a lot of the layout-level control but you're in a language that's fast to iterate in and easy to generate.

The other piece is the feedback loop. A DSL for models should be designed around fast compilation, good error messages, and easy profiling, because the way a model gets good at this is by trying something, measuring it, and trying again. If a compile takes minutes or the error is a cryptic PTX assembler message, you've thrown away most of the benefit. The language and the tooling are kind of inseparable here.

And honestly, I think the hardest part is not the language, it's the verification. Models can write code that looks great and is subtly wrong, especially around numerics, race conditions, and edge cases on sequence lengths. So I'd want the DSL to make correctness easy to check, with reference implementations, differential testing, maybe some lightweight formal guarantees about memory safety. If you get that right, I'm fairly optimistic that a lot of kernel engineering becomes a search problem, with the model as the search, and the humans working on the parts that are genuinely new: new algorithms, new hardware, deciding what's worth optimizing in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts models with humans: models tolerate verbosity and boilerplate but struggle with implicit hardware knowledge. It uses those differences to argue for explicit, inspectable DSLs designed for models.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting question is: what should the model have to figure out, and what should the compiler take care of? If you’re generating a GPU kernel, you probably want the model thinking about the algorithm, how to break up the computation, and how to move data efficiently. You don’t necessarily want it spending all its effort on low-level details that a compiler can handle reliably.

As models improve, that boundary can move. They might become much better at working with a lower-level language. But I don’t think that makes abstractions irrelevant. A good abstraction still makes the search space smaller and makes it easier to check whether something is correct.

So I’d think about the language and the feedback loop together. Can the model write something, compile it, test correctness, benchmark it, and then improve it? You want enough control to express fast implementations, but also a short, reliable path from an idea to a measurement. And I’d be careful about designing too narrowly around the mistakes today’s models make, because those might not be the same limitations six months from now.

r001.rationale: The response discusses dividing work between a model and a compiler, but does not identify differences between how language models and humans operate as a reason to design DSLs around models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting question is: what’s the right level of abstraction for the model? If you make the language very high-level, it’s easier to generate something correct, but you might restrict the optimizations it can express. If you make it very low-level, you give it more control, but now it has to get a lot more details right.

As models improve, that boundary can move. But I’d still want the compiler to handle things that we know how to do reliably. You don’t necessarily want the model spending its effort on register allocation. You want it exploring algorithmic choices, how to tile a computation, how to organize the work, and then getting feedback from actually running it.

So I’d think about the language and the feedback loop together. Can the model express an interesting optimization? Can it check correctness? Can it benchmark the result and understand what went wrong? A more capable model might use a more expressive language, but having good tools to test its ideas is still going to matter.

r001.rationale: The response discusses choosing an abstraction level for models and giving them compiler and benchmarking support, but it does not identify differences between how language models and humans operate as a reason for the DSL design.
